NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. said Sunday that it is buying troubled Wall Street firm Bear Stearns, amid deepening fears that Bear's demise could have sent shockwaves across already shaky financial markets. The deal to buy Bear Stearns is worth an estimated $236 million. The deal values Bear Stearns at $236 million, or just $2 a share. Shares had closed at $30 on Friday, down 47 percent that day. "Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations," said a statement released Sunday by JPMorgan. Shareholders must approve the deal, which is expected to close by the end of June. JPMorgan is taking immediate responsibility for Bear's trading obligations and assuming "management oversight" of the firm's operations. The deal has already been approved by the Federal Reserve and other regulators, according to the statement. The Fed is providing special emergency financing for up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets. "JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive of JPMorgan. "Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk," he continued. The fast-track deal is expected to close by the end of June, the statement said. Bear Stearns was on the brink of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said they would provide the brokerage a short-term loan. Bear was dealing with a classic "run on the bank." The firm's short-term creditors refused to lend the firm any more money and simultaneously demanded repayment of outstanding debt. The one-two punch overwhelmed Bear's cash position. With the global credit crisis worsening, the Fed -- along with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies -- took the dramatic action to prevent the investment bank from going under and igniting widespread panic through the financial markets.  Watch a discussion on the impact on global markets » . Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said on Sunday that talks about how to rescue Bear had continued throughout the weekend. He defended the Fed's bailout on Friday as "the right decision" and said the Bush administration was ready to take other actions to bring stability to the financial markets. He would not say what might have happened had the government failed to step in. "I'm not going to speculate about what-ifs," he said. "I'm just going to say our clear priority right now -- our number one priority, everything we're doing in the economic arena -- is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy." Bear Stearns has approximately 14,000 employees worldwide. The deal marks an inglorious chapter for 85-year-old Bear Stearns, a storied Wall Street firm the unraveling of which has been fast and furious. Rumors that Bear Stearns was on the verge of collapse started buzzing around Wall Street trading desks last Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz -- who took over as CEO in early January from longtime chief Jimmy Cayne -- appeared on television on Wednesday afternoon to reassure the markets that the firm was stable. But by Thursday night, Bear was in a severe crunch. Some firms that trade with it effectively stopped offering it credit because they feared that Bear was running short of short-term funding, or liquidity. "The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns," said Alan Schwartz, president and CEO of Bear Stearns. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances." White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson has briefed U.S. President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve's role in helping to facilitate the purchase. "We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening," said Fratto. "Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments." Shares of Bear Stearns opened last week at $69.75 and traded as high as $159 last year. E-mail to a friend .

**NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com)** — In a bid to avert a catastrophic disruption across fragile global markets, JPMorgan Chase & Co. announced Sunday that it has agreed to acquire the embattled Wall Street firm Bear Stearns. 

The emergency acquisition values Bear Stearns at approximately $236 million, or just $2 per share—a staggering drop for a stock that had closed on Friday at $30 after plummeting 47 percent in a single trading session.

"Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations," JPMorgan said in an official statement released Sunday. The deal, which has already received regulatory approval from the Federal Reserve and other agencies, remains subject to shareholder approval and is expected to close by the end of June. 

To facilitate the buyout, the Federal Reserve is providing special emergency financing to back up to $30 billion of Bear Stearns’ assets. 

"JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of JPMorgan. "Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk."

The swift resolution follows a dramatic downfall for the 85-year-old investment bank, which employs approximately 14,000 people worldwide. By Friday, Bear Stearns was on the brink of complete financial collapse, prompting JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to step in with a temporary emergency loan. 

The firm succumbed to a classic "run on the bank": as market confidence eroded, short-term creditors simultaneously refused to extend new credit and demanded immediate repayment of existing debt. This liquidty squeeze rapidly overwhelmed Bear Stearns’ cash reserves. 

With the broader credit crisis deepening, the Federal Reserve—alongside officials from the Treasury Department and other government bodies—took unprecedented action to prevent a collapse that threatened to ignite widespread panic throughout the financial system.

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson confirmed Sunday that high-level rescue talks continued throughout the weekend. Defending the Fed's emergency intervention on Friday as "the right decision," Paulson affirmed that the Bush administration stands prepared to take further measures to restore market stability. 

Refusing to speculate on what might have transpired had the government failed to intervene, Paulson stated: "I'm not going to speculate about what-ifs. I'm just going to say our clear priority right now—our number one priority, everything we're doing in the economic arena—is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy."

White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Secretary Paulson had kept President George W. Bush fully briefed on the Federal Reserve's role in facilitating the acquisition. 

"We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening," Fratto said. "Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments."

The deal caps an inglorious chapter in the history of Bear Stearns, whose unraveling was remarkably swift. Speculation regarding the firm's liquidity began circulating across Wall Street trading desks early last week. On Wednesday afternoon, Chief Executive Alan Schwartz—who succeeded longtime CEO Jimmy Cayne in early January—appeared on television to reassure investors that the firm's financial position was stable. 

However, by Thursday evening, Bear Stearns faced a severe crisis as several trading counterparties, fearing a cash shortage, effectively halted credit lines to the firm.

"The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns," said Schwartz, President and CEO of the firm. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances."

The magnitude of Bear Stearns' collapse is highlighted by its recent stock performance: shares opened the week at $69.75 and had traded as high as $159 within the past year.

# JPMorgan Chase Rescues Bear Stearns in Emergency Federal-Backed Acquisition

In an extraordinary effort to prevent a systemic collapse of the broader financial markets, JPMorgan Chase has agreed to acquire the beleaguered investment bank Bear Stearns. The emergency buyout values the historic Wall Street firm at approximately $236 million, or just $2 per share—a dramatic price tag that underscores the severity of the firm's sudden distress.

### A Rapid Liquidity Crisis
The acquisition comes as Bear Stearns suffered an unprecedented and swift liquidity crisis. Over a matter of days, market confidence in the firm evaporated, leading to an immediate financial emergency. Short-term creditors began demanding full debt repayments while simultaneously refusing to extend further loans or rollover existing lines of credit, effectively cutting the firm off from the short-term capital required to fund its daily operations.

### Immediate Intervention and Federal Backing
To mitigate the fallout and prevent panic from spreading throughout the global financial system, JPMorgan Chase has stepped in with immediate operational support. Effective right away, JPMorgan has assumed management oversight of Bear Stearns and officially guaranteed all of the firm’s trading obligations. This step is intended to reassure counterparties and keep the broader trading ecosystem functioning smoothly.

The transaction is heavily backed by federal interventions. Recognizing the danger a collapse would pose to the national economy, the Federal Reserve agreed to support the acquisition by providing up to $30 billion in emergency financing. This federal backstop will cover Bear Stearns' illiquid assets, insulating JPMorgan from the most volatile portfolio risks associated with the deal.

### Next Steps and Regulatory Status

**Title:** Saved from the Brink: How JPMorgan and the Fed Stemmed the Fall of Bear Stearns

In mid-March 2008, the global financial system teetered on the edge of a catastrophic meltdown. Bear Stearns, a storied 85-year-old Wall Street investment bank, found itself at the epicenter of a rapidly accelerating subprime mortgage crisis. Heavily exposed to toxic mortgage-backed securities and reliant on short-term overnight loans to fund its daily operations, the firm suffered a sudden and fatal loss of confidence from its counterparties. Within days, a classic "bank run" unfolded in the wholesale lending markets. Lenders refused to roll over Bear Stearns' debt, and clients withdrew billions in cash. Faced with a severe liquidity crisis, the firm was mere hours away from declaring bankruptcy.

Recognizing that a chaotic collapse of Bear Stearns would trigger a domino effect across interconnected global markets, the U.S. government stepped in. Over a tense, high-stakes weekend, Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke and New York Fed President Timothy Geithner brokered an unprecedented rescue package. Because the Fed lacked the legal authority to bail out a non-bank financial institution directly, it required a solid commercial partner. Enter JPMorgan Chase, led by CEO Jamie Dimon. 

To facilitate the transaction and absorb the immense risk of Bear Stearns’ illiquid assets, the Federal Reserve agreed to provide emergency financial backing. The Fed created a special purpose vehicle (later known as Maiden Lane LLC) to take on $30 billion of Bear Stearns' most troublesome mortgage-backed securities, insulating JPMorgan from the worst of the toxic assets. 

With this safety net in place, JPMorgan agreed to acquire Bear Stearns for an initial, astonishingly low price of $2 per share—valuing the entire firm at roughly $236 million. For a company whose stock had traded at over $170 per share just a year prior, the sale price reflected the sheer severity of its distress and the toxic nature of its balance sheet. (The price was later raised to $10 per share to appease disgruntled Bear Stearns shareholders, but the initial agreement signaled to the world the dire nature of the crisis.)

The speed of the deal was crucial. Before Asia-Pacific markets opened on Monday morning, JPMorgan had to step in and explicitly guarantee all of Bear Stearns' trading obligations and financial liabilities. JPMorgan executives immediately assumed operational oversight of the firm, placing managers on Bear’s trading floors to calm terrified counterparties and oversee daily clearing functions. 

By guaranteeing Bear Stearns' trades, JPMorgan successfully stopped the run on the bank. The emergency acquisition provided immediate short-term stability, averting a widespread panic that threatened to freeze global credit markets and trigger a systemic collapse. 

While the merger prevented an immediate catastrophe in March 2008, it ultimately served as the opening chapter of the Great Recession. It demonstrated the extreme fragility of the modern financial system and foreshadowed the even larger shocks that would rock the global economy later that year, culminating in the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers six months later. Nevertheless, the rapid, Fed-backed rescue of Bear Stearns remains one of the most dramatic and consequential emergency interventions in modern financial history.

The outlet was uniquely positioned to bridge the gap between elite high-finance professionals and Main Street consumers. While institutional traders stared at complex Bloomberg Terminals, millions of readers tuned into **CNNMoney** on their computers and smartphones to understand how the market's swings would affect their retirement funds, mortgages, and daily lives.

Operating from **New** **York** gave the platform an unparalleled front-row seat to history. During the dot-com crash of the early 2000s, the catastrophic 2008 Great Recession, and the subsequent record-breaking bull market, **CNNMoney** journalists were on the ground. They walked the streets of Lower Manhattan, interviewed CEOs in corporate skyscrapers, and provided real-time breaking news as financial institutions rose and fell.

Beyond stock tickers and corporate earnings, the **New** **York**-based newsroom expanded the definition of financial coverage. **CNNMoney** stood out by exploring personal finance, technology trends, real estate markets, and the human side of business, proving that financial news didn’t have to be dry or exclusionary.

Although the brand eventually evolved into CNN Business as part of a broader corporate rebranding, the legacy of **CNNMoney** remains an iconic chapter in modern business journalism. It proved that in a city as relentless and dynamic as **New** **York**, clear, accessible, and fast-paced reporting is the ultimate currency.

**THE WALL STREET CHRONICLE**

**JPMorgan to Buy Bear Stearns for $2 a Share in Emergency Fed-Backed Deal**

**By David Miller**
**NEW YORK — March 17, 2008**

In an unprecedented Sunday night rescue engineered by the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Department of the Treasury, JPMorgan Chase & Co. has agreed to acquire failing rival Bear Stearns Cos. for a fire-sale price of just $2 per share. 

The emergency takeover, announced late Sunday before Asian markets opened, marks a dramatic fall from grace for Wall Street’s fifth-largest investment bank and underscores the deep severity of the ongoing global credit crisis. 

The deal values the 85-year-old firm at roughly $236 million—a staggering 99 percent drop from its peak stock price of $170 per share just over a year ago, and a brutal discount from its Friday closing price of $30.00. 

To facilitate the buyout and prevent a broader systemic meltdown, the Federal Reserve took the extraordinary step of agreeing to guarantee up to $30 billion of Bear Stearns’ most illiquid mortgage assets. In a separate move on Sunday, the central bank also slashed its discount rate by a quarter-point to 3.25 percent and opened its discount window to major Wall Street brokerages—a power not exercised since the Great Depression.

"JPMorgan Chase stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase. "Bear Stearns’ clients should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing their counterparty risk. We recognize the last week has been a difficult time for them, but we are confident in our ability to integrate this business seamlessly."

The dramatic acquisition follows a panicked 72 hours on Wall Street. Rumors regarding Bear Stearns’ liquidity erupted last week, driven by heavy exposure to risky subprime mortgage-backed securities. By Thursday, a modern-day "bank run" was underway as hedge funds, institutional clients, and credit counterparties rushed to pull their cash and business from the firm. 

By Friday morning, Bear Stearns was forced to seek emergency government intervention to stay afloat over the weekend, setting off a frantic round-the-clock race to find a buyer before financial markets reopened on Monday. 

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson voiced strong support for the transaction late Sunday, emphasizing that protecting the broader economy was the primary objective. 

"I appreciate the leadership shown by JPMorgan Chase and the Federal Reserve," Paulson said in a statement. "Rebuilding confidence in our financial markets is our top priority, and the actions taken today were necessary to maintain stability."

For Bear Stearns' 14,000 employees, the deal is a catastrophic blow. Employees and executives hold roughly 30 percent of the company's stock, meaning billions of dollars in personal wealth evaporated over the weekend. Massive layoffs are widely expected as JPMorgan begins integrating the firm's trading, investment banking, and prime brokerage units.

As trading desks prepare for the opening bell this morning, panic remains palpable across global markets. Dow futures tumbled overnight, and Asian indexes dropped sharply as investors grappled with the realization that a major U.S. financial institution could collapse in a matter of days.

While the Fed's aggressive backing of JPMorgan has temporarily neutralized the immediate threat of a Bear Stearns bankruptcy, nervous investors are left asking a chilling question: Which Wall Street firm could be next?

Just fourteen months ago, the common stock of Bear Stearns Cos. traded at an all-time high of $171.36. Today, the 85-year-old Wall Street powerhouse—a firm that survived the Great Depression, the crash of 1987, and the dot-com bust—was sold for the price of a subway swipe. 

In a breathtaking, sleep-deprived weekend of high-stakes drama, JPMorgan Chase & Co., under pressure from the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury, agreed to acquire Bear Stearns for a meager $2 per share. The total price tag for the nation’s fifth-largest investment bank: $236 million. To put that figure into perspective, Bear Stearns’ iconic, 45-story skyscraper headquarters on Madison Avenue is estimated to be worth at least four times that amount.

The stunning collapse marks the most dramatic chapter yet in the subprime mortgage crisis that has gripped global finance for the past eight months. But what transpired at Bear Stearns over the past five days was not merely a story of bad real estate investments. It was a modern, high-speed execution of a classic financial terror: a run on the bank.

---

### The Anatomy of a Modern Bank Run

To understand how a firm with $395 billion in assets could be rendered worthless in less than a week, one must abandon the 1930s image of frantic depositors lining up around the block to withdraw paper currency. 

Bear Stearns did not take retail deposits. Instead, like much of modern Wall Street, it relied heavily on short-term, secured loans—known as repurchase or "repo" agreements—to fund its daily operations. Every night, Bear was forced to borrow tens of billions of dollars to pledge against its securities, promising to buy them back the next day. 

The strategy works brilliantly when markets are calm. But Bear Stearns had a fatal vulnerability: it was heavily exposed to toxic subprime mortgage-backed securities. Last summer, two of Bear’s internal hedge funds imploded due to bad subprime bets, dealing a severe blow to the firm’s reputation. 

By last week, as the mortgage market continued to rot, whispered rumors began to circulate across trading desks: *Bear is running out of cash. Bear can’t cover its obligations.*

In finance, perception is reality. On Wall Street, confidence is the only currency that truly matters. Once it evaporates, insolvency is only a matter of hours away.

---

### Five Days in March: The Death Spiral

The terminal crisis began in earnest on Monday, March 10. Rumors surged through the financial district that major counterparties were pulling back from Bear. 

Seeking to quell the growing hysteria, Bear Stearns Chief Executive Alan Schwartz appeared on CNBC on Wednesday morning, declaring that the firm’s "liquidity position and balance sheet have not been materially altered." He assured investors that Bear held a comfortable cushion of $17 billion in cash reserves.

The market did not care. 

By Thursday, March 13, the panic was absolute. It was a classic domino effect, executed at the speed of fiber-optic cables:
* Big hedge funds, terrified that their assets would be frozen if Bear filed for bankruptcy, began transferring their accounts to rival firms like Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.
* Major banks refused to extend short-term repo loans to Bear, demanding more collateral or outright refusing to accept Bear’s mortgage backed securities.
* Counterparties began demanding cash margin payments to cover trades.

By the close of business Thursday, Bear’s $17 billion liquidity buffer had vanished, draining down to just $2 billion. The firm was functionally dead. It did not have enough cash to open for business on Friday morning.

Late Thursday night, Schwartz called Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke and Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson with a chilling message: Without immediate government intervention, Bear Stearns would be forced to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy before sunrise.

---

### The Emergency Lifeline and the Weekend Huddle

Fearing that a Bear Stearns bankruptcy would trigger a catastrophic chain reaction—freezing the global credit markets and pulling down other institutions—the Fed took an unprecedented step. 

Before dawn on Friday, March 14, the Fed invoked emergency powers not used since the Great Depression (Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act) to channel an emergency loan to Bear through JPMorgan Chase. 

The move bought Bear 48 hours, but it failed to calm the market. Bear’s stock plummeted 47% on Friday alone. It was clear that a temporary loan was not enough. Bear needed a permanent buyer before Asian markets opened on Sunday evening, or a systemic meltdown would ensue.

Teams of accountants, lawyers, and executives converged on JPMorgan’s headquarters at 270 Park Avenue. Working around the clock, ordering pizza, and operating on virtually no sleep, JPMorgan’s CEO, Jamie Dimon, evaluated Bear’s toxic books. 

Dimon was willing to play savior, but only on his terms. He refused to take on the staggering, unquantifiable risk of Bear’s illiquid mortgage assets without a massive safety net.

Enter the U.S. government. To push the deal over the finish line, the Federal Reserve agreed to provide $30 billion in non-recourse funding to backstop Bear’s most troubled assets. In effect, the Fed is taking the toxic debt onto its own balance sheet to protect JPMorgan from catastrophic loss.

Furthermore, Treasury Secretary Paulson pushed hard for a low purchase price. The Bush administration was determined not to be seen as using taxpayer backing to bail out Wall Street executives and shareholders. 

The resulting price was a humiliating $2 per share—down from $30 on Friday, and $57 just a week ago.

---

### Shock, Grief, and the Shadow of Contagion

This morning, the mood at Bear Stearns’ headquarters was described by employees as a cross between a funeral and a war zone. 

Bear’s employees, who were encouraged to keep their savings in company stock, owned roughly 30% of the firm. Today, life savings, retirement funds, and college funds were wiped out in a single stroke. Junior analysts and veteran managing directors alike were seen leaving the building in tears, clutching cardboard boxes filled with personal belongings. 

"We built this house over eight decades, and it burned down in three days," said one weeping senior trader, who asked not to be named. "I’m holding stock that’s worth less than the coffee I bought this morning."

While the immediate threat of a Bear Stearns bankruptcy has been neutralized, the financial world is left reeling. The Fed’s aggressive intervention has prevented an immediate systemic crash, but it has shattered the long-held assumption that Wall Street’s premier investment banks were too big to fail.

As trading floors digest the reality of the $2 buyout today, a single, terrifying question hangs over lower Manhattan: 

If a run on the bank can destroy Bear Stearns in less than a week, who is next? All eyes on Wall Street are now nervously turning toward Lehman Brothers.

# JPMorgan to buy Bear Stearns in $2-a-share fire sale

### In an unprecedented move backed by the Federal Reserve, JPMorgan Chase agrees to buy its crumbling rival for just $236 million to avert a global financial panic.

**By Ellis Targett, CNNMoney.com staff writer**  
**NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- March 16, 2008: 9:12 PM EDT**

In an emergency move aimed at preventing a catastrophic collapse of the U.S. financial system, JPMorgan Chase agreed late Sunday to acquire embattled investment bank Bear Stearns for a shockingly low $2 a share. 

The deal values the 85-year-old Wall Street powerhouse at approximately $236 million—a staggering 93% discount from its closing price of $30 on Friday, and a far cry from its all-time high of $170 per share just a year ago.

The buyout, brokered in intense over-the-weekend negotiations between top Wall Street executives, federal regulators, and the Bush administration, represents one of the most drastic interventions in Federal Reserve history. 

To facilitate the deal, the Fed took the extraordinary step of agreeing to provide up to $30 billion in financing to backstop Bear Stearns’ most toxic, illiquid assets—effectively placing taxpayer money on the line to absorb potential losses.

"JPMorgan Chase stands behind Bear Stearns," Jamie Dimon, chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase, said in a statement released Sunday evening. "Bear Stearns' clients should be condident that JPMorgan Chase will stand behind the terms and performance of Bear Stearns' obligations."

### A historic collapse

Bear Stearns (BSC), the fifth-largest investment bank on Wall Street, was brought to its knees in less than a week due to a classic, modern-day run on the bank. 

Long considered one of the heaviest players in the high-risk mortgage-backed securities market, Bear suffered massive losses as the U.S. housing crisis worsened over the past year. As rumors about its solvency mounted last week, institutional clients, hedge funds, and counterparties rapidly withdrew their funds and refused to trade with the firm, draining Bear's cash reserves.

By Thursday night, Bear Stearns Chairman Alan Schwartz was forced to inform the Federal Reserve that the company would not have enough cash to open for business on Friday morning without emergency help. 

"The past week has been an extraordinarily difficult time for Bear Stearns," Schwartz said Sunday. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies given the recent severe liquidations we faced."

### The Fed steps in

Recognizing that a chaotic bankruptcy filing by Bear Stearns could trigger a domino effect, pulling down other major banks and shutting down global credit markets, the Fed stepped in with emergency funding early Friday. When that failed to calm nervous investors—sending Bear's stock tumbling 47% in Friday trading—the central bank gave JPMorgan 48 hours to orchestrate a complete buyout before markets opened in Asia on Monday morning.

Alongside the deal announcement on Sunday night, the Federal Reserve took two additional emergency actions:
*   **Discount Rate Cut:** The central bank lowered its emergency lending rate (the discount rate) for commercial banks by a quarter-percentage point to 3.25%.
*   **Primary Dealer Credit Facility:** The Fed opened its emergency discount window directly to major Wall Street investment firms (primary dealers) for the first time since the Great Depression, allowing non-banks to borrow directly from the Fed against collateral.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson voiced strong support for the Fed's actions late Sunday. 

"I appreciate the additional actions taken tonight by the Federal Reserve to enhance liquidity and stability in our financial markets," Paulson said in a statement. "I am confident that our financial institutions and markets are resilient and flexible."

### Market fallout expected

Despite the deal, shockwaves are expected across global markets on Monday morning. Investors are grappling with the reality that a major Wall Street institution could vanish almost overnight, raising deep concerns about who might be next.

U.S. stock index futures dropped precipitously following the announcement, with Dow Jones industrial average futures falling more than 300 points in Sunday night trading. Overseas, Asian markets opened sharply lower, with Tokyo's Nikkei index down nearly 3% in early trading.

Wall Street analysts were stunned by the low price tag of $2 per share, which essentially wipes out Bear Stearns' equity shareholders, including many of its own employees who hold roughly 30% of the firm's stock. 

"This isn't a merger; it's a rescue mission," said Peter Boockvar, equity strategist at Miller Tabak & Co. "The price tag tells you everything you need to know about the quality of the assets on Bear's balance sheet. The Fed clearly believed that if Bear went into bankruptcy tonight, the system might not have survived tomorrow morning."

The acquisition is expected to close in the second quarter of 2008, subject to shareholder approval—though given the Fed's guarantees and JPMorgan's immediate assumption of Bear's trading obligations, the deal is effectively a done deal.
